_doc: Authored T-0462 findings for the second 75-person pass. Omitted cohort members received documented no-corroboration outcomes; candidates are never household facts.
default_summary: No reliable record found in the reviewed contemporary, institutional, local-history and index searches could be tied to this person by more than the recorded name. This is a documented no-find, not evidence that the person did not exist.

bates_john_jr.summary: The 1843 Chicago directory identifies John Bates Jr. as an auctioneer at 174 Lake Street, independently extending the exact-name and trade match beyond Andreas.

beaubien_jean_baptiste.summary: The United States Supreme Court record says John Baptiste Beaubean of Cook County paid $94.61 on 28 May 1835 for 75.69 acres. It directly supports his Cook County identity and land claim; it does not resolve conflicting retrospective cabin dates.

beaubien_josette.summary: Citizen Potawatomi Nation identifies Josette LaFromboise as Francis LaFromboise's daughter and Jean Baptiste Beaubien's wife. The relationship is corroborated; her exact roof on 1 July 1835 remains inferred.

beaubien_madore.summary: Citizen Potawatomi Nation identifies Madore as the 1809 son of Jean Baptiste Beaubien and Mahnawbunokwe and describes his later interpreting work. A tree-only marriage lead was not imported.

beaubien_mark.summary: Chicago History Museum's encyclopedia independently gives Mark Beaubien's 1826 arrival from Detroit and merchant and tavern roles. It strengthens the biography but does not establish his exact 1835 roof.

caldwell_billy.summary: Institutional histories corroborate Billy Caldwell's Chicago leadership and place the westward removal in 1835. This conflicts with Andreas/project language placing migration in 1836 and is retained as a dated conflict.

calhoun_john.summary: The Encyclopedia of Chicago independently identifies John Calhoun as founder of the Chicago Weekly Democrat in 1833 and operator of the city's earliest press.

clybourne_archibald.summary: The Encyclopedia of Chicago places Clybourn's slaughterhouse at the city limits from 1827 and describes his 1830s door-to-door meat trade, corroborating occupation while preserving its outside-town location.

couch_ira.summary: Chicago History Museum and WTTW independently connect Ira Couch to the Tremont House. Later summaries differ on when management began, so Andreas's earlier 1834 evidence remains qualified rather than replaced.

hamilton_richard_j.summary: A digitized Cook County history identifies Richard Jones Hamilton as clerk and recorder from county organization in 1831 and later probate judge, treasurer and school commissioner.

hogan_john_s_c.summary: The edited 1835 Illinois incorporation act names John S. C. Hogan as a Chicago corporate trustee. The exact unusual initials, office, place and date independently resolve the identity.

kinzie_john_h.summary: The Papers of Abraham Lincoln records John Harris Kinzie's 1829 Winnebago agency appointment, permanent Chicago settlement in 1834 and village presidency.

kinzie_juliette.summary: Wisconsin Historical Society identifies the Fort Winnebago agency house as John and Juliette Kinzie's 1830–33 residence and corroborates her authorship of Wau-Bun.

robinson_alexander.summary: The 1833 treaty and Indigenous Chicago corroborate Alexander Robinson's treaty and trading roles and Des Plaines reserve. Current scholarship conflicts with the household's doubtful 1762 birth and by-1816 arrival; exact Wolf Point presence remains inferred.

robinson_catherine.summary: Indigenous Chicago identifies Catherine Chevalier as Robinson's Potawatomi wife, married in 1826, and records her parents and grandfather. These relationships are used because sourced, not inferred from names.

owen_thomas_jv.summary: A primary Abraham Lincoln payment record attests Owen's Chicago house; institutional papers and a county biography identify wife Emeline Hotchkiss and four sons. The sources do not fix their address or occupancy on the scene date.

pearsons_hiram.summary: A contemporary reminiscence describes Pearsons as a house painter who entered real estate. This corrects the household's unsupported treatment of speculator as attested: house painter is sourced; investor or speculator is interpretive.

peck_philip.summary: Chicago History Museum's encyclopedia and period histories identify Philip F. W. Peck as a Providence-born merchant and real-estate developer arriving in July 1831. Spelling varies Phillip/Philip.

porter_jeremiah.summary: Presbyterian Historical Society corroborates Porter's 1833 Chicago mission and church organization; a Rochester notice records his 15 June 1835 marriage to Eliza Chappel. Their 1 July whereabouts remain uncertain.

porter_eliza_chappel.summary: Chicago Historical Society and school records corroborate Eliza Chappel's publicly funded school work and 1835 marriage. The separate 'Eliza Mir Chappel' letter record is a merge candidate pending inspection of the original column.

snow_george_w.summary: Chicago Historical Society records Snow's December 1833 election as assessor and surveyor. Its memorial attribution of balloon framing conflicts with the Encyclopedia of Chicago's description of that attribution as a popular myth.

spring_giles.summary: The Papers of Abraham Lincoln gives Spring's relocation to Chicago in June 1833, Franklin and South Water law office, 1836 partnership and marriage, improving the household's year-only arrival.

taylor_augustine.summary: Chicago History Museum identifies Augustine Deodat Taylor as designer and builder of St. Mary's in 1833 using balloon-frame construction, while keeping him distinct from brother Anson who hauled lumber.

temple_john_t.summary: A municipal preservation study corroborates Temple's July 1833 arrival with wife and four children and his mail contract, but gives dwelling and office locations that conflict with the household. Addresses remain unresolved.

wright_john.summary: Chicago Public Library distinguishes storekeeper John Wright from son John Stephen and dates their joint arrival with merchandise to 29 October 1832 and Prairie Store at Lake and Clark.

bailly_joseph.summary: Honoré Gratien Joseph Bailly de Messein is a strong regional candidate, but lived at his Porter County homestead and died there in December 1835. A Chicago letter may reflect transit, not residence.

candidates.name: Honoré Gratien Joseph Bailly de Messein
candidates.basis: Exact shortened name, regional trade network and matching period.
conflicts: Documented Porter County residence; no source links him to this letter.

chappel_eliza_mir.summary: The entry is a near-certain duplicate of Eliza Chappel Porter: Mir likely misreads Miss, and the letter appeared 16 days after her marriage. It is not merged until the original scan is inspected.

candidates.name: Eliza Chappel Porter
candidates.basis: Exact maiden name, unique Chicago chronology and title-like transcription.
conflicts: The scan is unavailable; Mir-to-Miss remains unverified.

curtenius_fredk.summary: Frederick William Curtenius is a possible candidate who moved to Michigan and farmed at Grand Prairie in 1835. The middle initial conflicts and no Chicago bridge was found.

candidates.name: Frederick William Curtenius
candidates.basis: Distinctive surname, age and same-year westward chronology.
conflicts: Middle initial differs and the source supplies no Chicago link.

parcel_aaron.summary: Aaron Parcel and Aron Parcell are reciprocal duplicate candidates: one-letter spelling variants occur in returns ten months apart, but no external discriminator was found.

candidates.name: Aron Parcell letter-list record
candidates.basis: Near-identical uncommon name in the same post-office corpus.
conflicts: Different return dates and no linking record.

parcell_aron.summary: Aron Parcell and Aaron Parcel are reciprocal duplicate candidates. The spelling and shared post-office context are suggestive but insufficient to merge.

candidates.name: Aaron Parcel letter-list record
candidates.basis: Near-identical uncommon name in the same post-office corpus.
conflicts: Different return dates and no linking record.

murray_alonzo.summary: Alonzo Murray and Alonzo Murry are strong duplicate candidates from one-letter variants in consecutive-year Chicago returns; no independent identity record resolves them.

candidates.name: Alonzo Murry letter-list record
candidates.basis: Exact given name and one-letter surname variant in the same post-office corpus.
conflicts: No external bridge.

murry_alonzo.summary: Alonzo Murry and Alonzo Murray are strong duplicate candidates but remain separate until a record or scan links the spellings.

candidates.name: Alonzo Murray letter-list record
candidates.basis: Exact given name and one-letter surname variant in the same post-office corpus.
conflicts: No external bridge.

brooks_gardner.summary: A Des Plaines history places Gardner Brooks among settlers along the river in 1833. Exact uncommon name, Cook County and chronology are useful, but no record links him to this letter.

candidates.name: Gardner Brooks of Des Plaines
candidates.basis: Exact uncommon name, Cook County and 1833 settlement.
conflicts: No direct link to the Chicago post-office entry.

burdick_paul.summary: Milwaukee history says Paul Burdick occupied a frame house raised there in March 1835. Exact name and date make a regional candidate, while Milwaukee residence conflicts with physical Chicago presence.

candidates.name: Paul Burdick of Milwaukee
candidates.basis: Exact name, Great Lakes region and same-year residence.
conflicts: Milwaukee residence; no linking Chicago record.

case_nehemiah.summary: A Buffalo directory supplies a competing Nehemiah Case, but wrong geography and no migration bridge make it a rejected match rather than a Chicago identity.

candidates.name: Nehemiah Case of Buffalo
candidates.basis: Exact name and period.
conflicts: Buffalo geography and no Chicago discriminator.

abbott_constant.summary: Dr. Constant Abbott is a strong regional candidate documented in DuPage and Ottawa by 1836, but no source supplies a dated Chicago migration or links him to this return.

candidates.name: Dr. Constant Abbott
candidates.basis: Rare exact name and adjacent-county chronology.
conflicts: No direct Chicago link.

covell_thomas_r.summary: A county history says Thomas R. Covell moved to Salt Creek, Cook County, about 1833 after work as trader and mill builder. Exact middle initial and migration make a high-confidence candidate, not town residence.

candidates.name: Thomas R. Covell of Salt Creek
candidates.basis: Exact full name and dated Cook County migration.
conflicts: Salt Creek lay outside Chicago town; no explicit link to the letter.

dow_albert_f.summary: An exact-name Albert F. Dow later served as Ottawa canal toll collector and eventually Chicago collector. The regional trajectory is compatible but lacks a link to 1835.

candidates.name: Albert F. Dow of Ottawa
candidates.basis: Exact name and later Illinois canal career.
conflicts: No 1835 migration or household bridge.

griswold_eben.summary: A Berrien County history names an Eben Griswold as a constable, but multiple exact-name candidates and no dated Chicago bridge prevent identification.

candidates.name: Eben Griswold of Berrien County
candidates.basis: Exact name and plausible regional geography.
conflicts: No chronology or identifier links him to the letter.

tuller_elam.summary: A county biography says Elam Tuller's family reached Chicago in July 1833 and identifies his Connecticut origin and farmer, mechanic and steam-engine manufacturing background. Two letter returns support the chronology.

sen_elijah_wentworth.summary: Cited local history and Wau-Bun identify Elijah Wentworth Sr. as a Wolf Point tavern keeper who later operated at Sand Ridge. Exact senior designation, occupation and chronology resolve him, but downtown scene-date presence is not proved.

filer_elihu_d.summary: Racine histories identify exact-name Elihu D. Filer as an early settler and carpenter, but no record bridges the Chicago letter to the Racine man. Reprinted OCR variants are not separate people.

candidates.name: Elihu D. Filer of Racine
candidates.basis: Exact full name, trade and regional chronology.
conflicts: No Chicago-to-Racine migration bridge.

house_chester.summary: A contemporary 1835 letter and local histories place distinctive-name Chester House at House's Grove from 1833. He is probably the recipient, but as a hinterland resident, not proof of Chicago residence; sources conflict on spouse name.

candidates.name: Chester House of House's Grove
candidates.basis: Rare exact name, contemporaneous land ownership and 1833 local claim.
conflicts: Hinterland residence; Judith versus Lucinda spouse conflict.

miner_amanda.summary: Kaneville history names Amos and Amanda Miner as first permanent settlers in 1836. Exact name, adjacent county and chronology support a candidate, but spouse and New York origin are not imported.

candidates.name: Amanda Miner of Kaneville
candidates.basis: Exact name, adjacent county and one-year chronology.
conflicts: No direct bridge to the Chicago letter; printed 2 counts letters, not people.

vann_angeline.summary: A later Missouri genealogy names an Angeline Vann born in 1834. The chronology makes her an impossible adult Chicago resident and the match is explicitly rejected.

candidates.name: Angeline Vann of Missouri
candidates.basis: Exact name only.
conflicts: Born 1834 and later Missouri geography.

fairchilds_ransom.summary: Ransom Fairchild of Connecticut and Michigan is a possible regional candidate, but the printed plural may be possessive OCR and no Chicago bridge exists.

candidates.name: Ransom Fairchild of Michigan
candidates.basis: Near-exact name and regional chronology.
conflicts: No Chicago link; name normalization unverified.

felch_alaneon.summary: Wisconsin Historical Society catalogs Alson Felch, later a Racine farmer. Alaneon-to-Alson cannot be asserted without scan confirmation or a Chicago-linked record.

candidates.name: Alson Felch of Racine
candidates.basis: Rare similar name and regional chronology.
conflicts: Given-name reading differs and no migration bridge exists.

ford_ebenezer.summary: A church history places Ebenezer Ford among Fort Dearborn garrison charter members in June 1833. This is a strong identity candidate; the resident record also omits his 20 May 1835 return before the 1 July return.

candidates.name: Ebenezer Ford of the Fort Dearborn garrison
candidates.basis: Exact name, Chicago institution and 1833 chronology.
conflicts: The roster does not explicitly identify the later letter recipient.

galusha_ezra.summary: Warrenville Historical Society says Ezra Galusha brought his family to Warrenville in 1834. The two Chicago letters fit postal routing, not bodily presence in town.

candidates.name: Ezra Galusha of Warrenville
candidates.basis: Exact uncommon name, nearby geography and 1834 arrival.
conflicts: No record directly links him to the letter; documented hinterland residence.

makepiece_george_r.summary: Will County history says George R. Makepeace explored future Joliet in June 1834, returned to New York, then returned with family. Exact initial and chronology are strong; spelling and letter linkage remain unproved.

candidates.name: George R. Makepeace of Joliet
candidates.basis: Near-exact rare name, middle initial and dated travel chronology.
conflicts: Makepiece/Makepeace variant unverified; no direct letter link.
